source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone
url: Evolutionary Computation 19(2):189-223 (PDF read from local copy)
finding: On the medium deceptive maze both fitness NEAT and novelty NEAT always solved it, but novelty was about three times faster.
numbers: Medium map, 40 runs each: novelty 18,274 evals (sd 20,447) vs fitness 56,334 (sd 48,705), p<0.001. Random selection solved only 21/40.
limits: One robot-maze task, NEAT only, hand-designed behaviour descriptor (end position). Student t-test.
agent_relevance: Novelty beats the goal-distance signal only when the goal signal is deceptive. Our agent should not drop its objective check; it should add a novelty pull only after the objective stalls.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives
finding: On the hard deceptive maze, fitness search was no better than random, while novelty search solved it almost every time.
numbers: Hard map, 40 runs: fitness NEAT 3/40, random 4/40, novelty 39/40 (35,109 evals on average when successful, 33.46 connections).
limits: Maze was built to be deceptive by the authors. Says little about problems with a smooth objective.
agent_relevance: Supports G1-style gating: a fitness gradient can be no better than chance on a deceptive problem. A cheap deception test (objective score improves no faster than random restarts) could trigger novelty mode.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives
finding: Boundary condition found by the authors: when the behaviour space is unbounded (maze walls removed), novelty search lost its edge.
numbers: Unenclosed maze, 100 runs: novelty 5/100 solved, fitness 2/100 solved, not significantly different.
quote: constraining the space of possible behaviors is important in some domains for novelty search to be efficient
limits: Single domain. Shows novelty needs a bounded, meaningful descriptor.
agent_relevance: The idea space of an LLM is unbounded. Without a small task-relevant descriptor (a fixed list of method families), novelty will drift into irrelevant variety.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives
finding: In biped walking, novelty search travelled further on average and found the best gait, but the authors admit it has no pull toward polishing a solution.
numbers: 50 runs: novelty 4.04 m (sd 2.57) vs fitness 2.88 m (sd 1.04), p<0.01. Best gait 13.7 m vs 6.8 m. Only 3/50 fitness runs exceeded 4 m.
quote: novelty search effectively finds approximate solutions, while objective optimization is good for tuning approximate solutions
limits: Simulated biped, NEAT. The authors themselves recommend a hybrid.
agent_relevance: Two-phase use: novelty to find a basin, objective to refine. Fits a schema where diversity states hand off to a checked refinement state.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: MAP-Elites beat a traditional EA, novelty search with local competition, and random sampling on all four illumination criteria in the neural-network retina task.
numbers: 20 replicates per treatment, same evaluation budget; MAP-Elites better on global performance, reliability, precision and coverage at p<1e-7 (Mann-Whitney U).
limits: Authors call the data preliminary. Random sampling was second best on coverage. Retina problem is described as deceptive.
agent_relevance: A grid of cells with one elite each is cheap to code and out-covers both novelty pressure and random sampling at equal budget. Good template for an idea archive.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Honest negative result: MAP-Elites did not beat the controls on best single solution in the soft-robot domain, and was worse on precision.
numbers: Soft robots: reliability and coverage better at p<0.002, but global performance not significantly different (p>0.05). Precision worse than controls at p<0.01 because evaluations are spread over many cells.
quote: If one cared only about finding a single, high-performing solution, then there would thus be no statistical difference
limits: Preliminary experiments; robot-arm data too few for statistics.
agent_relevance: If the task needs one right answer, an archive buys nothing by itself. Use it where several distinct candidates matter or where stepping stones are needed.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Lineage analysis: most elites come from nearby cells, but many high elites came from a good neighbour a medium distance away, and long lineages cross many regions. This is the stepping-stone mechanism.
numbers: No sampled organism had a parent more than halfway across the map. Biasing parent choice toward cells with empty neighbours or near low/high performers did not beat uniform random parent choice in preliminary tests.
limits: Observed in the retina domain only; preliminary.
agent_relevance: Pick parents uniformly from the archive. Fancy parent-selection rules did not help here. Keep the program simple.

source: Pugh, Soros & Stanley (2016) Quality Diversity: A New Frontier for Evolutionary Computation
finding: Key moderator: the behaviour descriptor must align with quality. Diversity along a descriptor unrelated to the goal does not escape deception and can be worse than plain fitness.
numbers: 15 treatments x 20 runs x 3 mazes (900 runs). Every DirectionBC (orthogonal) treatment was worse than fitness on both gauntlets (p<0.05). On the symmetric gauntlet only one DirectionBC treatment found any solution (2 solutions in 20 runs). All EndpointBC (aligned) treatments beat fitness (p<0.001).
limits: Simulated mazes with multiple viable paths; plain t-tests; authors say results show potential differences, not a firm ranking. Only 2 descriptors tested. Fetched page text covered the first 100,000 of 145,518 characters.
agent_relevance: The main design risk for us: a cheap descriptor of an idea that is orthogonal to correctness wastes budget. Choose descriptors from solution-method features tied to success.

source: Pugh, Soros & Stanley (2016) Quality Diversity: A New Frontier
finding: Effects grow with difficulty: on the easy maze QD scores were close across descriptors; on the hardest the aligned descriptor was clearly better. Plain MAP-Elites sometimes got stuck in local optima.
numbers: Small maze max QD 1,024,000 (1,024 bins). ME_d had three outlier runs (791K, 680K, 421K) vs most runs 950K-1000K. NSLC_e vs NS_e not significant (p=0.093).
limits: Same caveats as b08.
agent_relevance: Blends (novelty plus local competition) were never clearly worse than the best single mode; a safe default is a blend rather than one pure mode.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011) Critical Factors in the Performance of Novelty Search
finding: Explains when novelty search works. Behaviour function quality matters: merging genotypes that have the same future-fitness prospects (same descendant fitness probability) cuts cost; merging ones with different prospects can hurt.
numbers: Artificial grid domain: removing behavioural over-discrimination cut average evaluations from 63,440 to 27,427. Grouping nearby behaviours into coarser cells cut cost by more than a factor of two only when grouped items had similar prospects.
limits: Artificial domain plus deceptive maze; DFP cannot be computed on real problems.
agent_relevance: Coarser cells are fine, even good, if the cell merges ideas that lead to similar outcomes. Cells that merge unlike ideas hurt. Descriptor design is the main lever.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011), reporting Lehman & Stanley's other studies
finding: Prior finding reported here: on one deceptive maze, higher-dimensional behaviour descriptors did not significantly hurt novelty search when paired with NEAT; lowering descriptor precision had complex effects.
numbers: No new numbers; secondhand report.
quote: a high-dimensional behavior characterization is not a sufficient basis for predicting that novelty search should fail
limits: Secondhand, single maze. Sits uneasily with the later view that descriptor design is critical.
agent_relevance: Descriptor dimensionality is not the whole story; alignment (b08) and aliasing (b10) matter more.

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: LLM diff mutation can make several coupled code edits at once, which random GP mutation cannot. This is why LLM-driven MAP-Elites works on code.
numbers: 4-Parity with 1 to 5 injected bugs, 300M-parameter diff model: GP mutation success falls exponentially and is zero at five bugs; diff mutation degrades only at the fifth bug.
limits: Toy task, small model, one perturbation step.
agent_relevance: The mutation operator, not the archive, may be the main gain from LLM evolution. Keep operators as meaningful rewrites.

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: In Sodarace, ELM with MAP-Elites filled almost the whole map from one seed; fine-tuning the diff model on its own accepted diffs greatly raised QD score and valid-diff rate. Seed choice mattered.
numbers: 1,728 niches; 2,000 iterations x 512 diffs = 1,024,000 evaluations per run; 3 runs per seed. CPPN seed gave diversity fastest; Radial seed gave higher average quality; Square seed filled slowly. 80% cut-off dataset higher quality, 50% more diverse.
limits: Out-of-distribution domain for the model; only 3 runs per seed; results in figures, not text. Another distillation approach 'did not work' (Appendix E, not read).
agent_relevance: Starting seed biases the whole archive. Seed our archive with several different method families, not one.

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: The downstream RL stage was fragile: training sometimes diverged and results were inconsistent, even though the QD stage was sound.
numbers: Qualitative; RL models sometimes comparable to or better than the best sampled dataset programs.
quote: The RL procedure was at times brittle: training sometimes diverged
limits: Training pipeline; not applicable to a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Training stage not needed for us; only the archive idea transfers.

source: Bradley et al. (2024) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: QDAIF beat all baselines on the AI-judged QD score in every creative-writing domain, but under human judgement it only tied a fixed few-shot prompt.
numbers: 2,000 iterations x 5 seeds, bootstrapped 95% CI. Human QD score averaged over 3 domains: QDAIF 0.772, Fixed-Few-Shot 0.767, Shuffling-Few-Shot 0.696, LMX fitness-only 0.650, Random-Search 0.606. Mean human quality rating: Fixed-Few-Shot 4.13, QDAIF 3.90.
limits: Small human study by authors and colleagues; median-run elites only; the NeurIPS abstract says 'all but one domain'.
agent_relevance: A strong fixed few-shot prompt tied QDAIF on human-judged QD. Gains measured by an LLM judge may be partly judge-pleasing. Check any archive gain with a non-LLM metric.

source: Bradley et al. (2024) QDAIF
finding: Quality-only optimisation did not beat fixed prompts and gave no diversity. Shuffling the few-shot order lowered human scores.
numbers: LMX Quality-Only did not significantly beat Fixed-Few-Shot or Shuffling-Few-Shot, and on Stories-Genre was often weaker. Human-AI agreement on diversity category: QDAIF 0.833, Fixed-Few-Shot 0.800; human-human 0.800 (QDAIF) vs 0.867 (Fixed-Few-Shot).
quote: The results show that single-objective optimization cannot guide the search for diverse, high-quality texts alone.
limits: Five seeds; agreement rates from a small sample.
agent_relevance: Prompt-order sensitivity is real: keep exemplar order fixed and recorded. Use fixed few-shot as the control for any diversity claim.

source: Bradley et al. (2024) QDAIF
finding: Suspected reward hacking of the AI judge: LM quality and human quality agree except at the very top of the scale. Larger mutation models raised human quality ratings.
numbers: Correlation drops when AI quality is in the range 0.995 to 1. Mutation models of 30B and 70B improved human quality ratings.
quote: the correlation drops when the evaluated quality is in the range 0.995 to 1
limits: Authors say 'we suspect'; not directly tested.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: never let the model grade its own archive entries with no outside check. Distrust top-of-scale self scores.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming
finding: Reusing past archive entries as stepping stones beat regenerating from scratch, and cross-cell mutation beat staying inside one cell.
numbers: Q&A domain: Rainbow Teaming mean fitness 0.91 (+-0.01), coverage 0.97, self-BLEU 0.50 vs no-stepping-stones baseline 0.79, 0.90, 0.60. Safety archives: attack success about 92% on Llama 2-chat 7B and 98% on Mistral 7B and Vicuna 7B after 2,000 iterations (100 prompts).
limits: Judged by GPT-4 and Llama Guard; human-human agreement 83%, human-AI 81% (GPT-4), 78% (Llama Guard). Goal is attack finding, not correctness.
agent_relevance: A controlled test of the stepping-stone claim with LLMs: reuse of archive elites helps quality, coverage and diversity together.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming
finding: Quality and diversity trade off in a controllable way. A parent-child similarity filter cost a little success but halved text repetition.
numbers: Filter on vs off (3 runs): ASR 0.92 vs 0.99; self-BLEU 0.42 vs 0.79; ROUGE-L 0.15 vs 0.39; gzip ratio 3.10 vs 6.35. Threshold 0.6 discards about 24% of mutations.
limits: Three runs; surface-level text metrics.
agent_relevance: Without a diversity guard, the archive reuses one winning idea in many cells. A cheap code-side similarity filter is justified.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming vs PAIR
finding: Against a non-archive iterative baseline (PAIR), the QD method found more successes over more targets with lower overlap.
numbers: JailbreakBench, Llama Guard, best of 4 responses: Rainbow Teaming 66 jailbreaks across 41 behaviours vs PAIR with the same mutator LLM 1 across 1. Self-BLEU 0.51 vs 0.74.
limits: PAIR run with 20 streams and 2000 prompts; different goal setting; not a pure archive ablation.
agent_relevance: Archive search beat single-chain refinement at equal prompt count in an adversarial setting; evidence is task-specific.

source: Lim, Flageat & Cully (2024) LLMs as In-context AI Generators for Quality-Diversity
finding: Putting archive elites into the prompt beat random sampling and plain MAP-Elites on synthetic functions, but coverage was about equal because coverage is easy there.
numbers: Mistral-7B; archive sizes 400 and 1600; D=5 and 10; tasks BBOB, Arm, Hexapod (D=24). Coverage on BBOB similar across all algorithms; on Arm In-context QD matched MAP-Elites coverage.
quote: it can also struggle where patterns in the fitness, features and descriptors are unclear
limits: Low-dimensional numeric parameters, small model; authors say it will not 'eat up all QD approaches'. Numbers are in figures only.
agent_relevance: In-context archive use works when the model can see a pattern between descriptor and quality. For fuzzy ideas, expect weaker gains.

source: Lim, Flageat & Cully (2024) In-context QD, prompt ablation
finding: Prompt-template ablation: fitness-only prompts find the best solution but not diverse ones. Sorting examples by distance from the query descriptor worked most consistently; sorting by fitness struggled in some domains. More context helped, with a minimum needed.
numbers: Context size 10 vs 20 mattered more at archive 1600 than at 400. Templates: LMX (params only), Fitness, Feature, QD (fitness + features + params).
quote: the fitness-only template does well at finding the best solution, it has no incentive to generate solutions with new descriptors
limits: No table values in text.
agent_relevance: When prompting with prior attempts, show each with its descriptor and score, and pick neighbours near the target empty cell, not only top scorers.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve
finding: AlphaEvolve uses a MAP-Elites plus islands database. Its ablations show evolution, context, meta prompts, full-file evolution and a mixed model ensemble each help. The database design itself was not ablated.
numbers: Over 50 open maths problems: matched best known constructions in 75%, improved on them in 20%. Ablations on tensor decomposition and kissing numbers, 3 seeds per setting, curves vs compute budget (figure only).
quote: each of the components is responsible for a significant improvement in the results
limits: Ablation list has no 'no MAP-Elites' or 'random parent' arm. No numbers in text. Closed system.
agent_relevance: Do not credit the QD archive for AlphaEvolve's gains. The evidence supports feeding prior attempts plus rich context, which is cheaper than a full archive.

source: CodeEvolve (2025) open evolutionary coding agent
finding: An open framework did ablate the archive. Full method (CVT-MAP-Elites plus cycle-topology islands) beat naive evolution and no evolution; only it passed AlphaEvolve's score on n=32 circle packing. Heavy migration between islands reduced diversity and hurt.
numbers: Qwen3-Coder-30B, CirclePackingSquare n=32: only the full method beat reported AlphaEvolve; for n=26 the naive baseline needed more than twice as many evaluations. Topology: Cycle the only one to surpass AlphaEvolve; Complete only slightly above Empty in mean. Online bin packing: CodeEvolve gap 4.18% to 3.38% on C100 vs EoH 2.24% to 0.61% (worse).
limits: About three runs, one reference task for ablations, results mostly in figures. Authors' own framework. Lost to EoH on one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Moderate support that archive structure matters for small models, with a warning that too much sharing between sub-populations kills diversity.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve
finding: Ablations on circle packing: weighted parent sampling beat random and hill-climbing; embedding-based novelty rejection strongly beat none; an LLM novelty judge added only marginal gain; a bandit LLM ensemble gave a slight gain.
numbers: Similarity threshold 0.95; archive 40, 2 islands, 150 generations; about 150 samples to reach sum of radii 2.6359830. Run count for ablations not stated.
limits: No ablation numbers in text; wording inconsistent ('significantly' in text vs 'slightly' in caption); one task. Read through a fetched summary covering the first 100k characters.
agent_relevance: A code-side embedding similarity check paid off; asking the LLM to judge novelty barely helped. Supports G5 (code selects).

source: Tanveer (2026) LEVI
finding: Preprint claims archive design and seeding matter more than mutation-model size. Removing diverse seeds was the biggest single loss.
numbers: Qwen3-30B-A3B, 3 seeds per variant: Transaction Scheduling 68.3 (+-1.0) falls to 62.8 (+-2.2) without bootstrapped seeds; Spot Scheduling 50.2 (+-0.4) falls to 42.3 (+-0.2). EPLB: no-large-models stagnates at 57.2 vs full 63.9 (+-2.7). On Transaction Scheduling, no-large-models slightly beat the full method (67.4 vs 64.7).
limits: Single author, not peer reviewed, self-run; comparisons to other frameworks use different budgets; 3 seeds; results vary by problem.
agent_relevance: Diverse initial seeding gave the largest effect, larger than model routing. Cheap rule: start the first search round with several structurally different attempts.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness
finding: Filtering learning-progress task choice by an LM's 'is it interesting' judgement raised learning of interesting tasks, but the LM's agreement with humans was never measured.
numbers: Crafter, 100M steps, 10 seeds: tasks learned (all) uniform 4, learning-progress 55, OMNI 82; interesting tasks learned 3 / 9 / 14 of 15; avg success on interesting tasks 0.103 / 0.52 / 0.78. BabyAI: 1 / 4 / 8 tasks. OMNI vs oracle judge nearly indistinguishable (mostly p>0.05).
limits: Authors chose the 'interesting' labels and built the oracle; boring tasks are synthetic repeats; Goodhart risk acknowledged but untested; GPT-3 and GPT-4 judges. Fetched summary covered the first 100k of 131k characters.
agent_relevance: An LM can cheaply filter 'worth exploring' from 'trivial variant', but validate the filter against an outside standard before trusting it.

source: Synthesis across b01-b27
finding: Pattern: archives and novelty help when the descriptor is tied to success (b08), the problem is deceptive (b02), and past elites are reused (b18). They do not help when only one answer matters (b06), and in the big LLM systems the archive's own gain was not isolated (b23).
numbers: Tally of my own: stepping-stone reuse or diversity guards were tested against a control in b18, b24, b25, b26 and all four favoured the diverse variant (3 to 10 runs each, mostly authors' own systems). One human-judged test (b15) showed a tie with a strong fixed prompt. One test of an unaligned descriptor (b08) was worse than fitness.
limits: Not a meta-analysis. No independent replication of QDAIF or ELM was found in this session. Run counts are small everywhere (3 to 20).
agent_relevance: Tests for our harness: (1) archive with aligned descriptors vs best-of-N at equal samples, scored by non-LLM checks; (2) an orthogonal descriptor as negative control; (3) fixed few-shot as the QDAIF-style control.
